classification.difficultyReason: Two explicit parts guide a SAS proof and its side-equality consequence; students must select diagonal bisection and combine adjacent and opposite side equalities.

content.prompt: In the parallelogram $PQRS$ below, the diagonals meet at right angles at $M$.

spec.description: Unshaded parallelogram with double parallel arrows on PQ and SR, single parallel arrows on PS and QR, dashed diagonals and a right-angle marker at M. Ordinary marks use black; distinguished diagonals retain house red.
spec.mathematics: PQ parallel SR and PS parallel QR. The diagonal vectors (sqrt(10)-1,-3) and (sqrt(10)+1,3) have dot product zero. Both diagonals share midpoint M.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied parallel and perpendicular marks only; no derived side equalities are printed.

answer.short:
$\triangle PMQ\equiv\triangle RMQ$ by SAS.

$PM=RM$, $MQ$ is common and both included angles are right angles.
answer.worked:
$PM=RM$ (diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other).

$\angle PMQ=\angle RMQ=90^\circ$ (given perpendicular diagonals).

$MQ$ is common.

Therefore, $\triangle PMQ\equiv\triangle RMQ$ (SAS).

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence show that $PQ=RQ$, and so $PQRS$ is a rhombus.

answer.short: $PQ=RQ$ (matching sides). Opposite sides of the parallelogram are equal, so all four sides are equal and $PQRS$ is a rhombus.
answer.worked:
$PQ=RQ$ (matching sides of the congruent triangles in part a).

Also, $PQ=SR$ and $RQ=PS$ (opposite sides of a parallelogram).

Thus $PQ=RQ=SR=PS$, so $PQRS$ is a rhombus.

inlines.text: You have now proved the following test for a rhombus:
‘If the diagonals of a parallelogram are perpendicular, then the parallelogram is a rhombus.’
